analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or vote when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate three federal taxes on passing wealth between people: the estate tax owed when someone dies, the gift tax owed on large lifetime transfers, and a tax designed to stop families from skipping a generation to avoid estate tax. Repeal would apply to deaths and transfers after the law's enactment. The bill never moved past its initial referral to the tax-writing committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates and people planning to give away large sums while alive. In 1991 the estate tax only applied to estates well above the size of a typical family's holdings, so the benefit would go almost entirely to the wealthiest families, while the lost revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Heirs to the largest family fortunes

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the estate tax entirely, so no federal tax would be owed on the transfer of wealth at death after enactment [S2, S3].
Eliminates the gift tax, so large lifetime gifts between people would no longer be taxed [S2, S3].
Eliminates the generation-skipping transfer tax, which exists to prevent families from skipping a generation to reduce or avoid estate tax on very large transfers [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. Repealing three wealth-transfer taxes would remove federal revenue, which would have to be replaced through other taxes, more borrowing, or less government spending. The direct benefit would concentrate among families with multi-million-dollar estates.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes removes federal revenue that would otherwise have to be raised through other taxes or borrowing [S2, S3].
The taxes targeted for repeal apply only to large estates and large gifts, so the repeal's direct benefit flows to the wealthiest households while the replacement burden falls broadly [S2].
The bill contained no offsetting provisions; it simply repealed chapters 11, 12, and 13 of the tax code, which would have added to the federal deficit at the time [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the vast majority of households, the bill offered nothing directly — their estates were already small enough that the estate tax did not apply — while everyone shared the cost of lost federal revenue. The gains would have gone to a small group of very wealthy families. The bill had no offsetting revenue provisions, making the trade lopsided in favor of concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane introduced the bill on January 3, 1991, the first day of the 102nd Congress [S1, S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: General taxpayers were better off because the bill died: the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes stayed in place, and heirs to large estates gained no new exemption. The bill was never seriously pursued after introduction, so no industry campaign was needed to stop it — the committee simply declined to act.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers, who kept the estate tax

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: The committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation, chaired by Rep. Dan Rostenkowski (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans; the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee never considered it, and no Democrats signed on.

industries.note: Full repeal of the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes would have let the largest fortunes pass untaxed at death or by gift [S2, S3]. The public cost is the lost revenue that other taxpayers would have to replace.

industries.industry: Estate planning professionals (lawyers, wealth advisors, trust companies)
industries.note: These professionals are paid largely to manage estates around the tax rules the bill would erase, so repeal would shrink that business. Their loss has no meaningful effect on ordinary people's finances.
Repeal would remove three sources of federal revenue, leaving the Treasury to replace them through other taxes, borrowing, or spending cuts [S2, S3].
